pool.prompt: A technician cuts their hand on a strand wire; the foreman applies a bandage on site and the technician works the rest of the day without restriction. Is this recordable on the OSHA 300 log?
choices: Yes — any cut requiring a bandage is recordable
No — bandaging alone is first aid and does not meet the recordable threshold
Yes — any hand injury on an OSP job is automatically recordable
No — only injuries requiring hospital treatment are recordable
pool.explanation: Bandaging is explicitly listed as a first-aid measure. First-aid-only treatment does not meet the recordable threshold — the distinction is the treatment given, not how severe the injury looks. If the same cut required sutures, staples, or prescription medication, it would be recordable.

pool.prompt: A field technician falls from a bucket lift and is admitted to the hospital for an overnight observation stay. Per 29 CFR 1904.39, when must the employer report this to OSHA?
choices: Within 8 hours of the incident
Within 24 hours of the incident
Within 7 days — only fatalities are 8-hour reportable
No reporting required unless the worker cannot return to work within 7 days
pool.explanation: 29 CFR 1904.39 requires in-patient hospitalization to be reported to OSHA within 24 hours. A fatality is 8-hour reportable. These timelines apply to ALL employers regardless of size — including firms with 10 or fewer employees who are otherwise exempt from routine 300 log recordkeeping.

pool.prompt: A technician's vehicle drifts into a cone taper but misses the crew by 10 feet; no one is hurt and no equipment is damaged. Under federal OSHA rules, what must the employer do?
choices: File an OSHA 300 entry — a near-miss is recordable
Nothing is legally required — federal OSHA has no mandatory near-miss reporting requirement
Report the near-miss to OSHA within 24 hours
Complete an OSHA 301 incident investigation report
pool.explanation: Near-miss reporting is voluntary under federal OSHA rules. An event with no injury, illness, or death does not meet the recordable threshold and does not trigger 1904.39 severe-incident reporting. Most safety-conscious employers still maintain voluntary near-miss programs as a leading-indicator tool.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1904.7(a); OSHA Near Miss Reporting Systems guidance.

pool.prompt: What is the OSHA safety metric that counts incidents resulting in days away from work, restricted work activity, or job transfer to another position?
choices: TRIR (Total Recordable Incident Rate)
DART rate (Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred)
LTIR (Lost Time Incident Rate)
EMR (Experience Modification Rate)
pool.explanation: The DART rate is calculated from OSHA 300 log entries involving DART outcomes — the most serious tier of recordable incidents. Formula: (DART incidents x 200,000) / total hours worked, normalized to a rate per 100 full-time equivalent workers.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1904 — Recording and Reporting Occupational Injuries and Illnesses.

pool.prompt: An OSP contractor has 8 employees and believes they are completely exempt from OSHA recordkeeping. Is this correct?
choices: Correct — firms with 10 or fewer employees have no OSHA recordkeeping obligations
Partially correct — they are exempt from routine 300 log maintenance but must still report fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss within the 1904.39 timelines
Incorrect — all employers regardless of size must maintain the full OSHA 300 log
Correct — but only if they are in a low-hazard NAICS code
pool.explanation: The 10-or-fewer-employee size exemption covers routine recordkeeping (maintaining the 300 log and posting the 300A summary). It does NOT exempt employers from severe incident reporting under 1904.39 — that requirement applies to every employer regardless of size.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1904.1 (size exemption); 29 CFR 1904.39 (severe incident reporting — all employers).

pool.prompt: Which four incident types trigger the 29 CFR 1904.39 severe-incident reporting requirement, and what are their respective reporting windows?
choices: Fatality (8 hr); in-patient hospitalization, amputation, and loss of an eye (each 24 hr)
All four types share a single 24-hour reporting window
Fatality (24 hr); hospitalization, amputation, and eye loss (each 8 hr)
Only fatalities are reportable under 1904.39 — the other three are voluntary
pool.explanation: A work-related fatality must be reported to OSHA within 8 hours. In-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must each be reported within 24 hours. These are distinct, mandatory reporting windows that apply regardless of employer size.

pool.prompt: What distinguishes a RECORDABLE injury from a merely first-aid injury under 29 CFR 1904.7?
choices: The apparent severity of the wound as judged by the foreman

The type of medical treatment actually given — treatments defined as first aid (e.g., bandaging, over-the-counter medication at nonprescription strength) don't meet the recordable threshold, while sutures, prescription medication, or restricted work do
Whether the injury occurred during regular work hours
Whether the injured worker missed any part of their shift
pool.explanation: 29 CFR 1904.7 defines recordability by the treatment actually provided, not by how the injury looks. A deep-looking cut that only needs a bandage is first aid (not recordable); a minor-looking cut requiring sutures is recordable. This is a common point of confusion for field supervisors.

pool.prompt: Match each incident type to its OSHA reporting timeline under 29 CFR 1904.39.
pool.explanation: Fatalities require the fastest reporting window (8 hours) because of the severity and urgency. In-patient hospitalization, amputation, and loss of an eye each require reporting within 24 hours — all four apply regardless of employer size.
